title: Handouts and outside sources
objective: See how a downloadable handout and a link to someone else's site are treated — both leave the page, on purpose.

blocks.text: Two things do not belong inside the lesson body: files that were designed for paper, and pages that belong to other people. Both get a card that says plainly what will happen when you act on it.
A handout is something you take away

A PDF has a fixed layout. It does not reflow, so on a phone it is either unreadably small or requires constant zooming. Putting one inside a scrolling box gives you two scrollbars and a worse version of a document the browser already knows how to display well.

blocks.title: When a PDF is the actual lesson
blocks.text: Then it should not be a PDF here. It should be authored as lesson content so it reflows, can be searched, translated and read aloud. The PDF stays as the printable export.
Somebody else's page is a link, not a frame
Most sites refuse to be embedded, so a frame often shows nothing at all. And when it does work, their content ends up wearing our chrome, which is misleading. A labelled link is the honest version.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is a PDF not embedded as the lesson body?

choices.A: PDFs cannot be displayed in browsers
choices.B: Its layout is fixed, so it will not reflow on a small screen, and reading it in a scrolling box puts a scrollbar inside a scrollbar
choices.C: PDFs are always too large to load
choices.D: Browsers block PDF files by default

checkpoint.explanation: The problem is fixed layout. The browser's own viewer, in its own tab, handles zoom and search far better than a box inside our page.

checkpoint.prompt: What is the main reason external pages are linked rather than framed?

choices.A: Most sites block being framed, and framing makes their content look like ours

checkpoint.explanation: Both halves matter: it frequently does not work at all, and when it does it misrepresents whose material the reader is looking at.
